data.title: Apprentice Hunter
data.body_md: An apprentice hunter is a resident or nonresident certified at an FWP office or online. A person can certify as early as age 9 but cannot use a license until age 10. The certification lets the apprentice hunt some species while accompanied by a mentor without first completing a hunter education course, and is limited to **two years** before hunter education is required. An apprentice may not apply for or purchase a bighorn sheep, moose, mountain goat, mountain lion, or wolf license, or a hunting license/permit with a limited quota. See fwp.mt.gov/hunt/education/apprentice-hunter.

data.title: Armed Forces
data.body_md: A member of the regular armed forces of the United States, a member's spouse or dependent (as defined in 10-30-2115) who resides in the member's household, or a dependent who is a member of the armed forces of a foreign government attached to the regular armed forces of the United States, is considered a resident for Montana hunting, fishing, and trapping licenses.

data.title: How to Hunt Safely in Bear Country
data.body_md: Minimize the likelihood of encountering a bear — calling game and using scents may attract bears, and camps, cabins, and horses should be kept bear-proof with attractants minimized. Carry **bear spray** at the ready in an accessible holster and know how to use it; in sudden grizzly encounters bear spray has proven effective. Report encounters where a grizzly displayed aggressive or defensive behavior toward people, livestock, or pets to FWP at **1-800-TIP-MONT**, the U.S. Forest Service, or the nearest FWP bear management specialist (listed on the printed Bear Aware page). Simply seeing a grizzly is not necessarily a reportable encounter. In an actual emergency, phone **9-1-1**.

data.title: Bear Identification — Grizzly vs. Black Bear
data.body_md:
Black bear hunters must be able to tell the difference between a grizzly and a black bear, because **grizzly bears cannot be legally hunted in Montana**.

| | Grizzly Bear | Black Bear |
|---|---|---|
| Shoulder | Prominent shoulder hump | No shoulder hump |
| Face profile | Dished | Straight |
| Ears | Shorter, rounded | Pointed, tall |
| Claws | Long, 2"-4" | Short, ~0.5" |
| Tracks | Longer claws, toes closer together | Shorter claws, toes more separated |

Color and size can be misleading — look for a combination of characteristics. **If in doubt, don't shoot.** Learn how to identify bears and be absolutely sure of your target.

data.title: Boats
data.body_md: A person may not use a motorboat or a sailboat for the purpose of killing, capturing, taking, pursuing, concentrating, driving, or stirring up any upland game bird, migratory bird, game animal, or fur-bearing animal until the motor is shut off and the progress of the vessel has ceased.

data.title: Bonus Point System
data.body_md: Bonus points offer additional drawing chances for first-choice drawings only. Bonus points are mathematically **squared** prior to the drawing: with 3 existing bonus points you receive 3² = 9 chances plus your original application, for a total of 10 chances (3² + 1).

data.title: Buy Bonus Points
data.body_md: In years you don't apply for a license, a bonus point can be purchased separately **between July 1 and Sept 30** to increase your chances for a future license or permit. Deer, elk, and antelope bonus points cost $20 (resident) / $25 (nonresident) per species. See fwp.mt.gov/buyandapply/hunting-licenses/bonus-points.

data.title: Carcass Disposal (CWD)
data.body_md: To prevent the spread of chronic wasting disease, all parts of the head or skull containing brain material and/or the spinal columns of deer, elk, and moose harvested in Montana must be left in the field at the kill site, or if transported for further processing, disposed of in a Class II landfill once that processing is complete.

data.title: Check Stations
data.body_md: All hunters are required by law to stop as directed at all designated hunting check stations on their way to and from hunting areas, even if they have no game to be checked.

data.title: Certain Combat Disabled Veterans
data.body_md: A veteran with certain combat-connected injuries may be entitled to half-priced licenses for deer and antelope. Up to **50 licenses** will be issued annually. Contact FWP Licensing for details at 406-444-2950.

data.title: Regulations Are Adopted by the Fish & Wildlife Commission
data.body_md: Regulations for season dates, structures, and restrictions were adopted by the Fish & Wildlife Commission on **December 4, 2025**, under the authority granted in MCA 87-1-301, and are **valid March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027**. The Commission reserves the authority to amend the seasons, limits, and regulations herein if deemed necessary for wildlife management purposes. Statutes and other agencies' restrictions are provided as a courtesy and do not fall under Commission authority. — Christy Clark, Director.

data.title: Dispose, Don't Expose
data.body_md:
**Don't dump carcasses.** There are three reasons not to dump a game carcass:

1. **It can spread CWD.** Once an animal with CWD dies, any part of the carcass can transmit the disease for at least two years.
2. **It's illegal.** Montana State Law prohibits dumping dead animals or refuse on public property, including all state-owned and managed lands, FWP-managed fishing access sites, and wildlife management areas — risking a fine and loss of hunting and fishing privileges for a year.
3. **It's unsightly.** A dumped carcass reflects poorly on the hunting community.

**Follow carcass disposal guidelines.** To prevent the spread of CWD, all parts of the head or skull containing brain material and/or the spinal columns of deer, elk, and moose harvested in Montana must be left in the field at the kill site or, if transported for further processing (including taxidermy or meat processing), disposed of in a Class II landfill once that processing is complete.

data.title: What Is Chronic Wasting Disease?
data.body_md: CWD is a progressive, fatal neurological disease that affects deer, elk, and moose. There is no known case of CWD affecting people, pets, livestock, or wildlife other than the deer family. However, the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommend not consuming meat from an animal known to be infected with CWD. The CDC also recommends that hunters have deer, elk, and moose tested if they were harvested in an area where CWD is known to be present, which includes hunting districts with, and adjacent to, those with CWD detections. Visit **fwp.mt.gov/cwd** for more information.

data.title: Where Is CWD?
data.body_md: CWD has been detected across much of Montana. Maps of where CWD is found are updated regularly and can be found at fwp.mt.gov/conservation/chronic-wasting-disease/in-montana.

data.title: Why Is CWD Management Important?
data.body_md:
Montana FWP has the responsibility for managing wildlife, which includes managing wildlife diseases. FWP's CWD management efforts:

- Help prevent long-term population declines in infected herds. Some states have seen more than a **40% decline in mule deer**.
- Decrease prevalence and likelihood of spread.
- Help mitigate the disease's broader impacts to Montana's hunting and outdoor legacy.

data.title: Definitions
data.body_md:
**General Deer/Elk Season:** typically five weeks long, mid-October through late-November; see hunting districts for specific dates by species.

**Game Animal:** deer, elk, moose, antelope, caribou, mountain sheep, mountain goat, mountain lion, bear, and wild bison.

**Hunt:** to pursue, shoot, wound, take, harvest, kill, chase, lure, possess, or capture, or the act of a person possessing a weapon (as defined in MCA 45-2-101) or using a dog or a bird of prey for the purpose of shooting, wounding, taking, harvesting, killing, possessing, or capturing wildlife.

**Shoulder Season:** a hunting opportunity conducted before or after the five-week general deer/elk season; see individual hunting districts.

**Migratory Game Bird / Upland Game Bird / Furbearer / Predatory Animal / Nongame Wildlife:** as classified by statute or rule.

**License / Permit:** an electronic or hard-copy document issued to an individual granting, or to be used in conjunction with the proper license to grant, the opportunity to hunt the specific species of animal.

**License Ambassador (formerly License Provider):** a third-party vendor offering self-service access to FWP's Online Licensing Service.

**Outfitter / Guide:** as defined in statute; a guide is employed by or contracted independently with a licensed outfitter.

data.title: Letter from the Director
data.body_md:
Last fall the Montana Fish and Wildlife Commission set the hunting regulations for 2026 and 2027, making changes to address concerns about nonresident hunting pressure and mule deer numbers.

Starting in 2023 FWP began reducing deer B licenses in areas with declining mule deer numbers, and the legislature limited most nonresidents to one deer B license (or two with a combination license). This fall the commission **reduced the number of deer licenses a resident can hold from eight to three**, made some deer licenses valid only on private land within most of the state, and passed a **cap on the sale of a particular nonresident deer license** — cutting roughly 2,500 of those licenses available to nonresidents.

Before the next biennial season-setting process, FWP will finalize a new mule deer management plan shaped by public feedback. Report unethical or illegal behavior at tipmont.mt.gov, and refresh your hunting ethics at fwp.mt.gov/itsuptous.

— Christy Clark, Director. *The **outside** is in us all.*

data.title: Antelope License for Hunters with a Disability
data.body_md: Individuals who are permanently physically disabled and nonambulatory (as defined in ARM 12.3.106) may apply for an antelope license. A total of **25 antelope licenses** are issued through the antelope drawing, offered in antelope hunting districts that have a total quota of 50 or more antelope licenses. Applicants must apply on FWP-provided forms at any FWP office; applications must be postmarked on or before **June 1**.

data.title: Resident With a Disability Conservation License
data.body_md: Residents certified as permanently and substantially disabled (as defined by FWP rules) who purchase a conservation license may also purchase a fishing license for half price (AISPP also required), and may purchase general deer, general elk, and/or upland bird licenses for half price. Applications are available at all FWP offices and the FWP website. The certification is valid for the life of the holder or until changed by the Montana Legislature.

data.title: Discrimination Prohibited
data.body_md: State and Federal laws — Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, the Age Discrimination Act of 1975, and Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 — prohibit discrimination on the basis of race, color, sex, age, religion, national origin, or disability. Anyone who believes they have been discriminated against may write to FWP Human Resources, 1420 East Sixth Avenue, PO Box 200701, Helena, MT 59620-0701, or the Office of Diversity, Inclusion and Civil Rights, U.S. Department of the Interior, 1849 C Street NW, Washington, DC 20240.

data.title: Disturbing Traps or Trapped Animals
data.body_md: A person may not destroy, disturb, or remove any trap or snare belonging to another person, or remove wildlife from a trap or snare belonging to another, without permission of the owner of the trap or snare. Between March 1 and Oct 1 a person may remove a snare from land owned or leased by that person if the snare would endanger livestock; this does not apply to a law enforcement officer acting within the scope of duty.

data.title: Dogs
data.body_md: It is unlawful to use dogs to chase game animals. Exception: dogs may be used to hunt mountain lions and spring black bears (see appropriate regulations) and to recover or locate wounded game animals, but handlers must maintain physical control of the dog at all times by means of a maximum 50-foot lead attached to the dog's collar or harness.

data.title: Donate a Hunting License to a Disabled Veteran
data.body_md: Residents and nonresidents can donate their Montana hunting license to a disabled military veteran or disabled active-duty service member working with an organization that uses hunting as part of the rehabilitation process. The recipient must be a Purple Heart recipient with a 70 percent or greater disability rating. Visit the FWP website for more information.

data.title: Donation Options
data.body_md:
When purchasing licenses you may donate to several programs:

- **Wolf Mitigation** — funds the Montana Department of Livestock's contracts with USDA Wildlife Services for wolf management (flight time, collaring, lethal control).
- **Warm Water Fisheries Enhancement** — supports projects that improve Montana's warm water fisheries and habitats.
- **Hunters Against Hunger** — covers processing and distribution of donated meat to feed hungry Montanans (mfbn.org/hunters-against-hunger).
- **MT-PLAN** — a DNRC grant program enhancing public access.
- **Bowhunters with Disabilities Program** — covers the cost of modified archery equipment for disabled hunters.

data.title: Drawing Applications
data.body_md: All applications for deer and elk permits must be submitted on or before **April 1**. Antelope, antelope B, deer B, and elk B applications must be submitted on or before **June 1**. Both resident and nonresident hunters are eligible to apply for most licenses awarded through the drawings. Drawings are based on the final quotas adopted by the F&W Commission, which may differ from those printed in these regulations. An email address is required of all applicants for limited licenses or permits.

data.title: Drawing Statistics & Bonus Points
data.body_md:
After each drawing, FWP publishes drawing statistics online showing the number of applicants in each category (resident landowner, nonresident landowner, resident, nonresident), the final quotas, and the number of successful applicants per opportunity, plus a detailed bonus-point report. **The quotas printed in these regulations may vary from the final quotas drawn based on biological surveys.** See fwp.mt.gov/buyandapply/hunting-licenses/drawing-statistics.

**How bonus points work:** every applicant gets one chance in the drawing; bonus points add "raffle tickets." Montana **squares** bonus points before the drawing, so chances grow exponentially. With 10 bonus points you get 101 chances — 100 for the squared points and 1 for the current application: (10 × 10) + 1 = 101. The system is designed to be completely random.

data.title: Evidence of Sex
data.body_md: A person who kills a game animal shall retain evidence of the sex of the animal with the carcass until it is processed. Evidence of sex does not need to be naturally attached.

data.title: Firearms
data.body_md: Firearms — including rifles, handguns, shotguns with 0, 00, or slugs, and muzzleloaders — and archery equipment are lawful for taking game animals; all other methods of take are prohibited. There is no rifle or handgun caliber limitation or magazine/round capacity restriction. Rifle scopes with illuminated reticles, built-in range finding, and "red dot" scopes are lawful. See specific muzzleloader requirements on the Weapons Restriction Areas page and the heritage muzzleloader season.

data.title: Fees and Refunds
data.body_md:
In addition to the cost of each permit or license, there is a **$5 nonrefundable application fee** for each license or permit you apply for. Prerequisite licenses (Conservation License, Base Hunting License, and AISPP) are also nonrefundable.

FWP may issue an **80% refund** for a Nonresident Combination License obtained through a drawing if returned prior to **August 1** and the start of the archery or general season; a **50% refund** is issued between August 1 and the start of the general season if the license has not been used. Nonresident license holders should call 406-444-2950. Other refunds require appropriate documentation:

| Reason | Deadline | Refund |
|---|---|---|
| Death of licensee | 12/1/26 | 100% |
| Death of immediate family member | 12/1/26 | 90% |
| Medical emergency | 12/1/26 | 90% |

data.title: Game Damage Hunt Roster Rules
data.body_md: The game damage hunt roster is a randomized list of hunters' names. If FWP identifies a need to implement a game damage hunt, roster hunters will be contacted by FWP. Sign-up for the game damage hunt roster is from **June 15-July 15, 2026**, and only on the FWP website through MyFWP.

data.title: Highlights
data.body_md:
- Resident deer hunters are limited to purchasing **three deer licenses** per license year (a general license and two B licenses, or three B licenses).
- Many mule deer B licenses are now **restricted to private land only** — check the opportunity-specific details for each hunt.
- Over-the-counter Deer B and Elk B license purchase date changed to **June 15**.
- Hunting and fishing licenses are accessible through the secure Montana MyFWP app, which stores licenses and digital carcass tags (E-Tags) that validate your harvest in the field.
- Photocopying or printing more than one license may constitute a violation; it is unlawful to apply for, purchase, or possess more licenses, permits, or tags than are authorized (see p.25).
- Permits for either-sex elk or brow-tined bull-antlerless elk limit the holder to antlered elk within only the designated hunting district for the period on the permit; antlerless elk hunting is not limited by the permit.
- Deadline for deer/elk permits and Nonresident Combination License applications is **April 1**.
- Nonresidents hunting with a Montana-licensed outfitter applying for combination licenses may purchase an additional outfitter preference point at application.
- To prevent the spread of CWD, follow the carcass disposal guidelines (see p.4).

data.title: Recovery and Possession of Horns and Skulls from Mountain Sheep
data.body_md: A person may recover and possess the horn(s) and attached skull, or portion thereof, of a mountain sheep that died of natural causes and was not purposefully or accidentally killed, captured, or taken. Horns and skulls recovered must be reported within 48 hours and presented to the department for inspection and placement of a permanent pin within 10 days ($25 pin fee). This does not allow recovery/possession found in state parks.

data.title: How To Use These Regulations
data.body_md:
Montana's 147,164 square miles is divided into **seven administrative regions**, each with a main regional office. Each region is broken into hunting districts numbered to match the region: Region 1 districts start with 1 or 001, Region 2 with 2 or 002, and so on.

**Before hunting you need to determine the following:**

| Question | Deer / Elk | Antelope |
|---|---|---|
| **What** species do you want to hunt? | Deer / Elk | Antelope |
| **Where** (find the hunting district) | Maps pp.32-43 | Maps pp.128-134 |
| **When** can you hunt? | HD regs pp.48-123; youth & PTHFV p.124; multi-district pp.126-127; hunting hours p.151 | HD regs pp.136-142; hunting hours p.151 |
| **How** do you want to hunt? | Archery (requires a Bow & Arrow License) or general weapon — see Laws & Rules p.23 and Weapons Restrictions p.28 | |
| **Required** licenses/permits & deadlines | License and Permit Types pp.12-13; Residency p.14 | |
| Know the legal **boundaries** | Restricted Area Descriptions pp.28-30 | |
| **Complete** the drawing application by deadline | Find the 5-digit code pp.48-123 | Find the 5-digit code pp.136-142 |

data.title: Hunter Harassment
data.body_md: It is unlawful to intentionally interfere with the lawful taking of a wild animal, or to disturb an individual engaged in the lawful taking of a wild animal with intent to prevent the taking.

data.title: Hunter Land Access
data.body_md:
**Private land** — Montana law requires permission for all hunting on private land, regardless of whether the land is posted. See FWP's Block Management Program (contact FWP at 406-444-3750); FWP publishes a Hunting Access Guide by Aug. 15 each year.

**Public land** — National Parks and National Park Service areas are closed to hunting. National Forests, National Wildlife Refuges, U.S. Forest Service, and BLM lands may have restrictions and closures; inquire at the local federal office. It is unlawful to post, place signs, or mark state or federal land other than by the managing agency.

**Railroads** — railroad right-of-ways are private property and may not be hunted or used for access without explicit permission.

**State School Trust Lands** — a Conservation License provides hunters, anglers, and trappers access to lawfully accessible State School Trust Lands during applicable seasons; additional requirements apply (DNRC 406-444-2074). Motorized travel is restricted to designated roads/trails; firearms may not be discharged within 1/4 mile of inhabited dwellings without permission.

**Stream Access Law** — does not allow hunting of game animals between the ordinary high-water marks of streams and rivers without landowner permission.

**State Parks** — some provide hunting; restrictions may apply (stateparks.mt.gov).

**Indian Reservation Trust Lands** — some reservations may offer opportunities with a tribal license; contact the appropriate tribal government (see Contacts, p.144).

data.title: Hunter Orange Requirement
data.body_md:
Any person hunting or accompanying a hunter for deer, elk, antelope, moose, bighorn sheep, mountain goat, black bear, or mountain lion during a firearm season must wear a **minimum of 400 square inches** of hunter orange (fluorescent) material above the waist, visible at all times.

Archery hunters during the Archery Only Season are exempt unless a concurrent firearm season is open in that hunting district.

data.title: Hunting Hours
data.body_md: Authorized hunting hours for taking game animals begin one-half hour before sunrise and end one-half hour after sunset each day of the hunting season. See the official Sunrise-Sunset Tables for your zone.

data.title: Incidental Harvest Resulting in an Unlawfully Taken Animal
data.body_md: If you or a member of your hunting party shoots an animal that results in an unlawfully taken animal, you should notify an FWP game warden or 1-800-TIP-MONT (1-800-847-6668) immediately and follow their instructions. **Hunters should field dress the animal but DO NOT transport the animal until you've received instructions.**

data.title: Indian Reservations
data.body_md: The F&W Commission has by rule closed all lands within the exterior boundaries of Montana's Indian Reservations to the hunting of game animals with the use of state licenses unless provided for in a cooperative agreement between the Tribal Government and the State of Montana. Contact FWP for current agreements.

data.title: Inspection by Warden
data.body_md: Game animals, game birds, fish, and fur-bearers taken must be shown to FWP Enforcement personnel for inspection when requested.

data.title: Interstate Wildlife Violator Compact (IWVC)
data.body_md: Montana is a member of the IWVC. Under the compact, member states recognize suspensions of hunting, fishing, or trapping privileges. It is unlawful for a violator whose privilege to hunt, fish, or trap is suspended to obtain or attempt to obtain a license, tag, or permit in a member state. For more information, call 406-444-2452.

data.title: Kill Site Verification
data.body_md: At the request of a Department Game Warden, it is required to return to the kill site of any game animal, game bird, wolf, or fur-bearer that has been hunted or trapped.

data.title: Landowner Permission
data.body_md: A person may not hunt or attempt to hunt fur-bearers, game animals, migratory game birds, nongame wildlife, predatory animals, upland game birds, or wolves while hunting on private property without first obtaining permission of the landowner, lessee, or their agents. This applies regardless of whether the land is posted. For purposes of this section, "hunt" also includes entering private land to (a) retrieve wildlife; or (b) access public land to hunt.

data.title: Landowner Preference
data.body_md: Montana landowners (resident and nonresident) may qualify for preference in the license/permit drawings for deer, elk, and antelope. Up to **15 percent** of final quotas may be set aside for landowner-preference applicants. Landowners or their designees apply by the applicable deadline and submit a separate landowner preference form: forms for **deer and elk permits** must be received by **April 1**, and forms for **Elk B, Deer B, Antelope, and Antelope B** must be received by **June 1**. A landowner must be eligible to hunt in the hunting district applied for.

data.title: Know the Facts About Lead
data.body_md: Lead particles from lead ammunition can be toxic if ingested and can poison wildlife scavenging from gut piles. Hunters can voluntarily choose to use non-lead, copper, or other high-weight-retention ammunition. To learn more, visit NonleadPartnership.org or HuntingWithNonLead.org. *FWP cannot regulate ammunition according to Montana statute; the law does not prohibit the use of lead ammunition.*

data.title: License Discount Opportunities
data.body_md: Montana resident members of the Montana National Guard, Federal Reserve, or Active Duty who participated after September 11, 2001, in a contingency operation outside the state for two months and have been released from active duty or discharged are entitled to a free Conservation License and a Fishing License. Youth, senior, and disabled discounts are shown on the Licenses Available Chart (pp.12-13).

data.title: License and Permit Possession/Use
data.body_md: A person may not apply for, purchase, or possess more than one license, permit, or tag of any one class or more than one special license for any one species. A person may not hunt unless carrying the required license or permit at the time, and must exhibit it and the identification used in purchasing it for inspection. A person may not alter, change, loan, or transfer any license to another person. The person to whom a license is issued shall validate it.

data.title: Antelope Licenses & Permits
data.body_md:
**Antelope License (either-sex)** — the total number of antelope licenses an individual may hold is limited to one, of which only one may be either-sex. Both residents and nonresidents may apply through the drawings; nonresidents are limited to 10 percent of the quota.

**Antelope B License (doe/fawn)** — the cost of the first nonresident antelope B license (through the drawing, over-the-counter, or surplus) is $200; additional nonresident antelope B licenses cost $150.

**Antelope Archery Only License (900/399, drawing only)** — valid for either-sex antelope with archery equipment only. Applicants must list the 900-20 (or 399-20) license as their **first and only choice**. Region 3 has a separate archery-only license.

data.title: Deer Licenses & Permits
data.body_md:
**General Deer License** — valid for one deer as indicated under the "General Deer License" heading on the hunting-district pages. Hunters may hold only one General Deer License; residents may buy a Sportsman's License, which includes one. Most nonresidents cannot buy a general deer license over the counter and must obtain one through a Big Game Combination, Deer Combination, or Landowner-Sponsored drawing.

**Deer Permit** — allows hunting in an otherwise restricted area or time period; must be used with a General Deer License. Residents must hold a General Deer License before applying; nonresidents must hold or apply for a Big Game or Deer Combination License.

**Deer B License** — usually for antlerless mule deer or white-tailed deer depending on the license type and hunting district, and allows harvest of a deer in addition to the general deer. **Resident deer hunters are limited to three deer licenses per year, only one of which may be a General Deer License.**

data.title: Elk Licenses & Permits
data.body_md:
**General Elk License** — valid for one elk. Hunters may hold only one. Most nonresidents obtain a General Elk License through a Big Game or Elk Combination drawing.

**Elk B License** — valid for taking an antlerless elk during a specific period in a particular district or group of districts; designed to control elk numbers and many are valid only on private land. Limited elk B licenses are drawn (deadline June 1); unlimited (UNL) elk B licenses have no sales limit and are available OTC. The only prerequisites are a Conservation License and Base Hunting License. **A hunter may possess a total of three elk licenses in a year, only one of which can be a General Elk License.**

data.title: License Validation/Tagging
data.body_md: When a person kills a game animal, before the carcass is removed from or the person leaves the site of the kill, take physical possession of the game animal by electronically validating the license or tag, or cutting out from the license or tag the date the animal was killed. A license or tag that is not electronically validated must accompany the carcass as long as any considerable portion remains unconsumed.

data.title: Littering
data.body_md: It is unlawful to dump or leave any garbage, dead animal, or other debris or refuse on any highway, road, street, or alley; on public property; within 200 yards of a public highway, road, street, or alley; or on privately owned property where hunting, fishing, or other recreation is permitted. A holder of a fishing, hunting, or camping license convicted of littering forfeits current licenses and the privilege to hunt, fish, camp, or trap for one year.

data.title: Marked or Radio-Collared Animals
data.body_md: It is lawful to shoot game animals that have radio collars, neck bands, ear tags, and/or other markers, but markers and radio collars must be returned to FWP. Please report the killing of a marked animal to the local FWP office.

data.title: Masking Human Odor
data.body_md: Artificial scents and Responsible Hunting Scent Association (RHSA) approved natural glandular scents may be used by hunters for the purpose of masking human odor. Urine-based and natural glandular scents are approved by the F&W Commission if they originate from a state or province not listed as having documented occurrences of chronic wasting disease, or from an RHSA-certified facility that displays the required marks (RT-QuIC Tested / DPP).

data.title: Motion-Tracking Devices
data.body_md: It is unlawful while hunting to use any electronic motion-tracking device or mechanism designed to track the motion of a game animal and relay information to the hunter (remote-operated cameras/video transmitting real-time information; seismic devices; thermal imaging; satellite and radio telemetry). A radio-tracking collar on a dog used by a hunter engaged in lawful hunting is not considered an unlawful motion-tracking device.

data.title: Motorized Vehicles
data.body_md: It is unlawful to hunt or attempt to hunt any game animal from any self-propelled or drawn vehicle (to be lawful, a hunter must have both feet on the ground and his/her body outside the vehicle; the Permit To Hunt From A Vehicle is the exception); to use a motorized vehicle to concentrate, drive, rally, stir-up, corral, or harass game animals; or to use a motor-driven vehicle off-road on state land. On state trust lands, motorized travel is restricted to designated roads/trails.

data.title: Muzzleloader Heritage Hunting Season Lawful Weapons
data.body_md: Plain lead projectiles and a muzzleloading rifle charged with loose black powder, loose pyrodex, or an equivalent loose black powder substitute, and ignited by a flintlock, wheel lock, matchlock, or percussion mechanism using a percussion or musket cap. The muzzleloading rifle must be a minimum of .45 caliber and may not have more than two barrels. The rifle may not use a cap/primer inserted into the open breech, be capable of being loaded from the breech, or be mounted with an optical magnification device.

data.title: Nonresident
data.body_md: A nonresident is eligible to purchase or apply for most Montana fishing, hunting, and trapping licenses. By state law, nonresidents are limited to, but not guaranteed, **10 percent** of the license and/or permit quota for a district. A nonresident unmarried minor, at least 12 (by Jan. 16, 2027) but not older than 17, may hunt and fish in Montana as a resident if the minor's parent, legal guardian, or parent with joint custody, sole custody, or visitation rights is a resident of Montana (see the Youth Hunter chart).

data.title: Nonresident Hunter Information
data.body_md:
Montana law governs nonresident hunters differently than residents:

- All nonresidents are limited to, but not guaranteed, **10% of the overall drawing quota** for an opportunity (a district with 100 permits allows nonresidents to draw only 10).
- The 10% cap includes both nonresident landowners and regular nonresidents; landowner preference is the first stage of the drawing and can account for up to 15% of total quotas.
- Nonresidents must be successful in the **nonresident combination drawing** before moving on to specific permit drawings. Combination licenses are drawn by preference points: applicants with the most preference points are drawn first, but Montana law reserves **25% of nonresident combination licenses for applicants with zero preference points** (MCA 87-2-115).

*Drawing-status meanings:* "**Released**" — initially unsuccessful in the primary phase but later successful from returned licenses. "**Unsuccessful**" with a zero preference-point balance — successfully drew a combination license in the primary drawing but elected to return it (which resets preference points to zero).

data.title: Nonresident Youth Combination License
data.body_md: Nonresident Youth Combination Licenses are sold to nonresident youth (ages 12-17) who have an adult immediate-family sponsor — a natural or adoptive parent, stepparent, grandparent, brother, or sister at least 18 years of age who possesses a current resident or nonresident deer or elk license. The youth must be accompanied by the sponsor while hunting. For details and an application, contact Licensing at 406-444-2950.

data.title: Obtain a License or Permit
data.body_md:
Only one license or permit of any type may be purchased each year unless otherwise specified (for example, a hunter may purchase more than one elk B license). Many licenses and permits may be purchased from FWP license ambassadors, FWP offices, or online licensing; some are available only through a drawing. Refer to the Licenses Available Chart (pp.12-13) for the full resident and nonresident list and application deadlines.

**Online licensing:** apply for and purchase many licenses at **ols.fwp.mt.gov**, generally between 5:00 a.m. and 11:45 p.m. Montana time. Montana residents can purchase resident licenses online or at a license ambassador with a valid Montana driver's license issued at least six months prior. All license purchases and applications are final and cannot be changed if drawn (ARM 12.3.601).

data.title: Off-Highway Vehicles (ATV, UTV, dirt bikes)
data.body_md: OHVs must be registered with the county treasurer and display a current off-highway permanent registration decal for off-road recreation on public lands. Resident hunters utilizing "summer motorized recreation trails" must purchase a summer motorized recreation trail pass ($20, valid two years). Nonresidents must obtain a nonresident temporary-use permit ($35, valid one calendar year).

data.title: Outfitters and Guides
data.body_md: A person may not act as an outfitter or guide, or advertise or represent to the public that the person is an outfitter or guide, without first securing a license. It is unlawful to engage in outfitting/guiding while not licensed, and unlawful to hire an outfitter or guide not licensed by the Department of Labor and Industry (call 406-841-2300).

data.title: Party Applications
data.body_md: In Montana a "party" means a group of **2-5 persons** applying together to obtain a license or permit. If successful, each hunter must harvest their own game. All party members must select the same opportunity type and the same bonus- or preference-point participation. For online applications, the party establisher lists all members and provides the party number to each; each member then applies online using that number. Bonus/preference points for party applications are the average of the members' individual points.

data.title: Possession of Wildlife Parts
data.body_md: A person may not possess, ship, or transport all or part of any game fish, bird, game animal, or fur-bearing animal that was unlawfully killed, captured, or taken, whether killed, captured, or taken in Montana or outside Montana. "Possess" includes capturing, taking, or retaining physical possession. Certain naturally-shed antlers, hides/heads/mounts of lawfully-taken animals, and bones of naturally-died animals are exempted as described.

data.title: Predatory Animals and Nongame Hunting
data.body_md: Predatory animals and nongame species can be hunted in Montana year-round without a license by resident and nonresident hunters. A Conservation License, or a State School Trust lands recreational use license, is required to hunt predatory and nongame animals on State School Trust Lands, and landowner permission is required on private land. Predatory animals: coyote, weasel, (striped) skunk, and civet cat (spotted skunk). Nongame species include badger, raccoon, red fox, hares, rabbits, ground squirrels, marmots, tree squirrels, porcupines, and prairie dog.

data.title: Preference Points
data.body_md: **75%** of Nonresident Combination Licenses are awarded to applicants in order of the greatest number of preference points; the other **25%** are awarded to applicants who hold no preference points, drawn at random. You do not have to apply to accumulate a preference point — select "YES" on the preference-point question and a **$100 fee** is added. All accumulated preference points, including one purchased at application, are used in the current drawing. Preference points are not reinstated if you successfully draw and then refund your Nonresident Combination License. **No one may hold more than three preference points.** A person who does not apply for a combination license may purchase one preference point for $100 between July 1 and Dec 31.

data.title: Permit to Hunt From a Vehicle (PTHFV)
data.body_md: Residents and nonresidents certified as permanently and substantially nonambulatory (as defined by state law) may apply for a Permit to Hunt From a Vehicle. Specific PTHFV field regulations apply. Applicants must apply on FWP-provided forms available at FWP offices or the FWP website; for more information contact FWP Licensing at 406-444-2950.

data.title: Permit to Modify Archery Equipment (PTMAE)
data.body_md: Residents and nonresidents certified as permanently and substantially disabled (as defined by FWP rules) may apply for a Permit to Modify Archery Equipment. The PTMAE allows a person with a disability to use archery tackle that supports the bow and draws, holds, and releases the arrow to accommodate the individual's disability. Arrows are not exempt and must meet the requirements for the Archery Only Season. This permit does not entitle the holder to use a crossbow during the Archery Only Season.

data.title: Public Roadways
data.body_md: It is unlawful for anyone to hunt or attempt to hunt any game animal on, from, or across any public highway or the shoulder, berm, barrow pit, or right-of-way of any public highway (the entire width between the boundary lines of every publicly maintained way when any part is open to the public for vehicular travel).

data.title: Recorded Animal Sounds
data.body_md: It is unlawful to use any recorded or electrically amplified bird or animal calls or sounds, or imitations of bird or animal calls or sounds, to assist in the hunting, taking, killing, or capturing of any wildlife except predatory animals, wolves, and those birds not protected by state or federal law.

data.title: Reminders
data.body_md:
- Youth and Apprentice Hunter information — see p.19.
- Game Damage Hunt Roster rules — see p.31.
- License Discount Opportunities — see p.18.
- Elk hunters can purchase multiple Elk B licenses — see p.16.
- Landowners or their designees apply online or at an FWP office, then submit a separate landowner preference form. Preference forms for deer and elk permits must be received by **April 1**; forms for Elk B, Deer B, Antelope, and Antelope B must be received by **June 1**.
- An email address is required of all applicants applying for limited licenses or permits.

data.title: Replacing a Lost License
data.body_md: Replacements of lost, stolen, or destroyed licenses or permits may be purchased online, at FWP offices, or from license ambassadors for a **$5 fee** per replacement license. The department will issue a replacement license when an animal is deemed unfit for human consumption due to disease or prior injury: the person must surrender the entire animal, may choose the same or the next license year, and must appear in person at an FWP regional office or headquarters in Helena during normal operating hours. Contact Licensing at 406-444-2950 or fwpgen@mt.gov.

data.title: Residency
data.body_md: To be a lawful Montana resident eligible to purchase resident fishing, hunting, and trapping licenses, you must: have been physically living in Montana for at least **180 consecutive days** immediately prior to purchasing a resident license; register your vehicle(s) in Montana; be registered to vote in Montana if registered to vote at all; not possess or have applied for any current resident hunting/fishing/trapping privilege in another state or country; and file Montana resident income tax returns if required to file. Once established, you must continue to meet all of these requirements and physically reside in Montana as your principal or primary place of abode for not less than **120 days** per year (days need not be consecutive). A person is not a resident if they claim residency in another state or country for any purpose, or are an absentee property owner paying property tax in Montana. An out-of-state driver's license is not acceptable ID for resident license purchases (MCA 87-2-105/87-2-106).

data.title: Restitution for Unlawfully Taken Wildlife
data.body_md:
Under Montana law a person convicted of, or who has forfeited bond or bail for, unlawfully killing, taking, or possessing game animals shall reimburse the state. Restitution amounts for a trophy animal:

| Species | Restitution |
|---|---|
| Bighorn Sheep | $30,000 |
| Elk | $8,000 |
| Antlered Deer | $8,000 |
| Moose | $6,000 |
| Mountain Goat | $6,000 |
| Antelope | $2,000 |
| Grizzly Bear* | $8,000 |

*No authorized hunting season. The F&W Commission may adopt more specific trophy criteria (minimum antler/horn measurements for elk, mule deer, white-tailed deer, and antelope).

data.title: Sale of Game Animals
data.body_md: A person may not purposely or knowingly sell, purchase, or exchange all or part of any game fish, bird, game animal, or fur-bearing animal, except that a person may sell/purchase/exchange hides, heads, or mounts of lawfully taken animals, and naturally-shed antlers with a skull or portion attached from an animal that died from natural causes (mount or purchase of a grizzly bear hide/head/mount is prohibited except as provided by federal law). Sale of meat is not allowed.

data.title: Simulated Wildlife
data.body_md: It is unlawful to discharge a firearm or other hunting implement at a simulated wildlife decoy in violation of any state statute, ARM, or F&W Commission rule regulating the hunting of the wildlife being simulated.

data.title: Identification Guide for Antelope, Deer & Elk
data.body_md:
**Antelope.** *Buck (Horned):* any antelope with a horn or horns at least 4 inches long as measured from the top of the skull (bucks have a distinctive black band under the lower jaw). *Doe/Fawn:* any antelope with horns less than 4 inches long.

**Deer** (applies to both mule and white-tailed species). *Antlered Buck:* a deer with an antler or antlers at least 4 inches long as measured from the top of the skull. *Antlerless:* a deer without antlers, or with antlers less than 4 inches long. Caution: antlers on mule and white-tailed yearling bucks may look similar.

**Elk.** *Antlered Bull:* any elk having an antler or antlers at least 4 inches long. *Antlerless:* a female or juvenile male with antlers less than 4 inches long. *Brow-tined:* any elk having an antler or antlers with a visible point on the lower half of either main beam greater than or equal to 4 inches long. *Spike Bull:* any elk having antlers that do not branch or, if branched, branch less than 4 inches long measured from the main antler beam. *Either-sex:* a male or female animal of any age.

data.title: SuperTag Lottery
data.body_md: Open to residents and nonresidents. Chances are sold electronically at all FWP license ambassadors and via ols.fwp.mt.gov for **$5 each**, for a chance at a hunting license for deer, elk, antelope, bighorn sheep, moose, mountain goat, and mountain lion. Each SuperTag license allows the winner to hunt in any Montana hunting district valid for that species, even if the district quota has been met. An individual may win one or a combination of SuperTags per year. Proceeds enhance public hunting access and FWP enforcement. Montana residents receive one free chance in a separate resident lottery for every General Elk or General Deer License purchased.

data.title: Free Licenses for Terminally Ill Youth
data.body_md: Montana law allows a terminally ill resident or nonresident youth under 18 years of age to receive a free one-time Deer and Elk Combination license (without bear), or a deer, elk, or antelope license/permit as applicable. The youth must be accompanied by a licensed outfitter or an adult licensed to hunt in Montana. Minimum age and hunter education requirements may be waived. For information, call Licensing at 406-444-2950.

data.title: Transport of Wildlife
data.body_md: An individual other than the license holder may transport lawfully taken, properly tagged game animals that comply with the Evidence of Sex requirements. It is unlawful to ship, possess, transport, or take out of state unlawfully killed game animals.

data.title: Traps
data.body_md: It is unlawful to destroy, disturb, or remove any trap or snare belonging to another person, or remove wildlife from a trap or snare belonging to another, without permission of the owner of the trap or snare.

data.title: 12-Hour Closure (Region 4 elk HD 424 & 442)
data.body_md: In Administrative Region 4, elk hunting districts **424 and 442** may be subject to a 12-hour closure for the antlerless portion of the general season. If the antlerless quota is reached, the general season reverts to only the brow-tined bull regulation until the end of the general season. Contact Region 4 Headquarters or the Augusta Check Station for updates at 406-562-3467.

data.title: Two-way Communication
data.body_md: The use of two-way electronic communication is prohibited while in the act of hunting game animals or wolves to aid in taking or locating live animals; while hunting mountain lion or bobcats with dogs beginning when the dogs are placed or physically released on tracks or a scent trail; to avoid game check stations or FWP enforcement personnel; or to facilitate unlawful hunting activity. Use for safety or other legitimate purposes is exempt. Includes radios, cell phones, text messages, and social media/apps.

data.title: Vehicle Killed Wildlife Salvage Permit
data.body_md: Carcasses and parts of elk, deer, antelope, and moose killed in vehicular collisions may be taken and possessed only with a Vehicle-Killed Wildlife Salvage Permit. No other game animals may be salvaged under this permit.

data.title: Waste of Game
data.body_md: Hunters, or persons in possession of a game animal or game animal parts, are prohibited from wasting or rendering unfit for human consumption any part of a game animal defined as "suitable for food." For game animals (excluding mountain lions), all four quarters including loin and backstrap are considered suitable for food.

data.title: Weapons Restriction Areas
data.body_md: Weapons restrictions are in effect in some hunting districts, stated in the license/permit description and/or with a specific date range. Equipment restrictions apply: **Archery** — see lawful archery equipment. **Crossbows** — lawful in weapons restriction areas unless an exception is noted. **Traditional Handguns** — not capable of being shoulder mounted, barrel length under 10½ inches, chamber only a straight wall cartridge. **Muzzleloader** — not capable of being loaded from the breech, no pre-prepared paper/metallic cartridges, charged with black powder/pyrodex, minimum .45 caliber, no more than two barrels. **Shotgun** — must be shouldered, breech- or muzzle-loaded, smooth bore and/or rifled barrel and/or rifled choke designed to fire shot or slugs.

data.title: Weed Control and Weed-Seed-Free Feed
data.body_md: Montana requires the use of certified weed-seed-free hay, grain, straw, mulch, cubes, and pelletized feed on state and federal lands. For more information, contact the Montana Department of Agriculture at 406-444-3144.

data.title: Youth Elk Permits and Elk B Licenses
data.body_md: Elk permits and Elk B Licenses issued only to youth **12 (by Jan 16, 2027) through 15 years of age** require the applicant to be within that age range at the time of application and to show proof of successfully completing hunter education. A youth 11 years of age who will reach 12 by Jan. 16, 2027, may apply for any special drawing after completing an approved hunter education course, and after Aug. 15, 2026, may hunt any game species for which their license is valid during an open season. In order to carry or use a firearm in public, a youth under 14 must be accompanied by a person having charge or custody of the child or under supervision as provided in MCA 45-8-344.

data.title: Youth Hunter
data.body_md:
**Special 2-day Youth Deer Hunt: October 15 & 16, 2026.** Lawfully licensed hunters **10 through 15 years of age** may hunt deer statewide during these two days with a general deer, deer permit, or deer B license, taking the deer species otherwise available on that license in the district being hunted. An adult at least 18 years of age must accompany the youth in the field. Shooting hours, hunter education requirements, and all other general-season regulations apply.

Some hunting districts offer additional special opportunities for youth ages 10-15 (see the district regulations and p.124). Youth who are 15 at the start of the general season may hunt in the youth areas with a general license even if they turn 16 during the season.

data.note: Includes Deer, Elk, State Lands, Upland Bird (excluding turkey) & Season Fishing licenses (with black bear). Conservation, Base Hunting, and AISPP fees also required.

data.name: Sportsman's Combination (without bear)

data.name: Military Recognition License
data.note: Must go through certification process only at FWP offices. No cost. Conservation License included.

data.name: Bonus Point (per species/license type)
data.note: Optional. Purchased at application or between July 1 and Sept 30. Deer/elk/antelope: resident $20, nonresident $25 per species.

data.name: Nonresident Combination Preference Point
data.note: Optional. Applies to the nonresident combination drawing (75% of licenses go to the most preference points; 25% to zero-point applicants). Purchasable July 1-Dec 31 if not applying.

data.name: SuperTag Lottery Chance
data.note: Open to residents and nonresidents. $5 per chance for deer, elk, antelope, bighorn sheep, moose, mountain goat, mountain lion. Proceeds enhance public hunting access and FWP enforcement.
